Fit the Smooth Block Around a Frozen Working Linearization

Source: R/statmod.R
fit_working.Rd

Runs the iteration of Fasola, Muggeo and Kuchenhoff (2018) for a term whose block is a working linearization with a frozen weight (modelterms7::jump() and modelterms7::jseg()). The smooth block is fitted exactly at the committed block, the break-points are read off the fitted coefficients and committed, and the two alternate until the read-off settles or the working objective stops moving.

Usage

fit_working(
  obj,
  beta,
  idx,
  spec,
  design,
  hyper,
  method,
  vb,
  tol,
  budget = 500L,
  stall_limit = 20L
)

Arguments

obj

The objective.

beta

The current stacked coefficients.

idx

The smooth block's indices.

spec

The specification.

design

The design.

hyper

The hyperparameters.

method

iwls() or an optimizer.

vb

The resolved verbosity.

tol

The alternation's tolerance, read for the objective-stall rule.

budget

How many working fits at most.

stall_limit

How many consecutive working fits with every unsettled break-point at its scaling floor end the phase.

Value

A list with the elements of fit_smooth(), where iterations is the total over the working fits and history is NULL, and with fasola, the number of working fits taken, and stalled, TRUE where the phase was ended by stall_limit. In the iteration proper the list also carries a note element, which is NULL.

Details

The two functions differ only in this sequencing, which is the sequencing of the segmented package. The fixed-point iteration to which these constructions belong is not a descent method on the objective of the model: its early steps under a large scaling factor move uphill on purpose, and in this way it leaves a spurious optimum. Embedding the read-off inside the objective of the inner optimizer would put a sufficient-decrease line search in its way and stall it. During the working fit the frozen blocks contribute \(X\beta\) and nothing else (st$working), which makes the inner fit the plain penalized working fit of the papers; the commit then advances the read-off, the scaling schedule and any relabeling of crossed break-point lineages, once per working fit.

Any inner method serves: the working fit goes through fit_smooth(), which takes iwls() or any optimizers7 optimizer, and the read-off never moves inside the objective of the inner method. The methods differ in cost. Each working fit is solved afresh at a frozen block, so a method that carries exact curvature closes it in a step or two, while a quasi-Newton method rebuilds its own curvature from nothing every time.

The exit is at a fixed point of the iteration or in the cycle into which it settles, judged on the working objective. The iteration stops when the read-off has settled (modelterms7::term_converged()) with the objective stalled, when the objective has stalled three times in a row, or when the objective equals its value two iterations back twice (the period-two cycle of the break-point that Muggeo documents, which a consecutive-change rule cannot detect). Only at a fixed point does the working objective coincide with the model's, so the fit does not keep a best-so-far iterate: mid-travel, the committed contribution of a good working value can sit orders of magnitude off the data. If the budget runs out, the verdict is FALSE.

A phase that cannot settle is ended early and reports FALSE as well. This happens where every break-point that has not settled sits at the floor of its scaling factor (modelterms7::term_stalled()) for stall_limit consecutive working fits: the factor can shrink no further, and there is nothing left with which to bring the break-point to rest. The profile objective of a discontinuous term is constant between consecutive observations, so such a break-point passes from one observation to the next for as long as the budget lasts. The default stall_limit of 20 ends such a phase, and the stall and cycle rules are read first at every working fit.

References

Fasola, S., Muggeo, V. M. R. and Kuchenhoff, H. (2018). A heuristic, iterative algorithm for change-point detection in abrupt change models. Computational Statistics, 33, 997–1015.
